items.title: Hermes Agent Usage Limits: Daily, Weekly and How to Check Them
items.content:
Hermes Agent usage limits changed on 27 October 2026. Nous Research announced on X that it had revamped Hermes Agent subscriptions: every new plan now includes a cloud agent, and usage has daily and weekly limits instead of one monthly block of credits. Below I explain what that means for you, how to check exactly where you stand with `/usage`, how limits work when you sign in with ChatGPT or Claude instead, and what Hermes does when a limit runs out, using the Hermes docs as the source. I’ve also added my video on Hermes Cloud below.

Key takeaways

- New Nous plans: daily + weekly limits, plus a cloud agent on every new plan.

- Check your limits any time with `/usage` (or `hermes usage` outside a chat).

- `/subscription` shows your plan; `/topup` shows your balance.

- When a limit runs out, Hermes can switch to a fallback model and park scheduled jobs.

- Want Hermes running without hitting walls? Claim a free strategy session.

## What changed with Hermes Agent usage limits

Before the revamp, a Hermes subscription worked like a monthly allowance: one block of credits that you used up over the month. If you had a heavy week early on, you could run dry long before the month ended.

The new plans split usage into daily and weekly limits. In practice, that spreads your usage across the month, so one busy day can’t burn the whole allowance. And every new plan now comes with a cloud agent included, so you can have a Hermes running 24/7 without setting up your own server.

Nous says existing subscribers can switch to the new plans at any time from the Nous Portal billing page. Hermes v0.22.5 (22 October) added support for these window-based plans in the app: plan gauges, limit cards, and recovery when you switch models after hitting a limit.

## How to check your Hermes usage limits

You don’t have to guess. Hermes gives you several ways to see where you stand:

Command
Where
What it shows

/usage
Any chat (CLI, Desktop, Telegram, Discord…)
Token use, cost breakdown, context window and, when your provider supports it, an Account limits section with remaining quota, credits or plan usage

hermes usage
Your terminal, no chat needed
The same account-limits block, ready for scripts (add –json)

/subscription
CLI
Your Nous plan, with a link to change it in the browser

/topup
CLI and messaging
Your Nous balance and billing on the portal (replaces the old /credits and /billing)

/insights
Any chat
Usage patterns over the last 30 days

Hermes also shows Nous credits notices in the status bar, such as usage bands and when a grant is spent. If they bother you, set `display.credits_notices: false` in config.yaml; `/usage` still works.

## Hermes usage limits when you sign in with ChatGPT or Claude

Not everyone uses a Nous plan. The providers page explains what each subscription actually pays for, and it’s the most common source of billing surprises:

- ChatGPT / Codex sign-in: `/usage` shows your Codex 5-hour and weekly windows. If you have usage-limit resets banked on your ChatGPT account, `/usage reset` redeems one and fully restores both limits. Hermes refuses while your limits aren’t used up, because spending a reset early wastes it; `/usage reset --force` overrides that.

- Claude Max sign-in: Hermes only works through the OAuth path on a Max plan with extra usage credits bought on top. Hermes uses those extra credits, not the base Max allowance. Claude Pro can’t use this path; you’d use an API key instead.

- OpenRouter: `hermes usage --provider openrouter` shows your credits.

If you’d rather not track five different rules, the docs point to Nous Portal: 300+ models under one subscription and one login.

## What happens when you hit a Hermes usage limit

This is where Hermes is smarter than most agents. When a provider says your limit is reached and tells Hermes when it resets, Hermes uses that information instead of retrying blindly:

- Fallback models: if you’ve set a fallback, Hermes moves to it and stays there until the reset time passes, instead of bouncing back and forth every turn.

- Scheduled jobs get parked: if a cron job’s provider reports its limit used up and every fallback is unavailable, the scheduler holds the job until the window reopens. You get one alert saying the job is held, not an alert every few minutes.

- Switching models: since v0.22.5, Hermes recovers when you switch to another model after hitting a plan limit.

The simple takeaway: set at least one fallback model, and your agent keeps working even on a day you’ve used up your main plan.

## How to make your Hermes usage last longer

Most usage goes on tokens, so the fixes are about sending fewer of them. These come straight from the docs’ tips:

- Run `/compress` during long sessions. It summarises the history and cuts the tokens sent on every turn.

- Use `/context` to see what’s filling the window: system prompt, tools, skills, memory or the chat itself.

- Run `hermes prompt-size` to see the fixed cost of every message before you even start.

- Send side jobs like image description and web summaries to a cheaper auxiliary model, instead of your main one.

- Start a fresh session with `/new` when you change topic.

Or just ask your agent: “Check my /usage, tell me what’s using the most tokens, and set up a fallback model so I don’t get stuck when I hit my limit.”

## Is the new plan better for you?

If your usage is steady, daily and weekly limits mean you’re far less likely to be locked out at the end of the month. If you work in bursts, such as one huge project day a week, the daily cap matters more, so watch `/usage` on those days and keep a fallback model ready.

Either way, the included cloud agent is the bigger change. It means a Hermes that keeps working while your laptop is closed, without paying for and managing a separate server.

## My verdict

The revamp makes Hermes usage easier to plan: limits that reset daily and weekly, a cloud agent on every new plan, and clear tools to see where you stand. Check `/usage`, set a fallback model, and you’ll rarely notice the caps. That’s everything you need to know about Hermes Agent usage limits right now.

items.title: Hermes Agent Slash Commands: The Complete Guide
items.content:
Hermes Agent slash commands are the shortcuts you type in a Hermes chat, starting with `/`, to control the agent without leaving the conversation: start a new session, switch model, run a task in the background, check your usage and much more. They work in the terminal, in Hermes Desktop and, for most of them, in Telegram, Discord and Slack too. There are dozens, so below I start with the ones worth learning first, then give the full list by category from the official slash command reference, and finish with what’s new: since v0.22.5, plugin commands can ask you to pick an option. I’ve also put my video on the /loop command below.

Key takeaways

- Type `/help` (or press Ctrl+P) to see every command.

- Learn these first: `/new`, `/model`, `/bg`, `/btw`, `/goal`, `/usage`.

- Any installed skill is a command too: `/<skill-name>`.

- Plugins can add their own commands, and now show pick-an-option menus.

- Want Hermes working for your business? Claim a free strategy session.

## How Hermes slash commands work

A slash command is a message that starts with `/`. Instead of going to the AI model as a question, it tells Hermes itself to do something: change a setting, start a task, show information. Most run instantly and don’t use any tokens.

You don’t need to memorise them. Type `/help` to see the commands grouped by category, or open the fuzzy command palette with `/palette` or Ctrl+P, start typing, and press Enter to drop the command into the message box. In messaging apps, `/commands` shows a paginated list.

## The Hermes slash commands worth learning first

If you only learn ten, learn these:

Command
What it does

/new [name]
Start a fresh session (alias /reset)

/model
Show or switch model, e.g. /model provider:model

/bg <prompt>
Run a task in a separate background session while you keep chatting

/btw <question>
Ask a quick side question about the chat without interrupting it

/goal <text>
Set a standing goal Hermes keeps working on until a judge model says it’s done

/queue <prompt>
Line up the next prompt without interrupting the current answer

/steer <prompt>
Slip a note in mid-task; the agent reads it after its next tool call

/compress
Summarise a long chat to save tokens

/usage
Token use, costs and your account limits

/stop
Kill running background processes

Two more that save a lot of time: `/retry` resends your last message, and `/undo` removes the last exchange.

## Session commands

These control the conversation itself:

- `/history`, `/save`, `/title`: view, save or name the chat.

- `/resume [name]` and `/sessions`: go back to an earlier session.

- `/branch` (alias `/fork`): copy the session to explore a different path. On Discord, Telegram, Slack and Matrix it opens in a new thread.

- `/rollback`: list or restore file checkpoints.

- `/diff`: show git changes in the working folder.

- `/snapshot`: save or restore your Hermes config and state.

- `/subgoal`: add a condition to the active /goal.

- `/heartbeat every <interval> <prompt>` and `/loop`: re-run a prompt on a schedule in this session.

- `/review`: spawn an independent reviewer for the work just discussed.

- `/moa <prompt>`: run one prompt through Mixture of Agents.

- `/refine`: run the memory and skill self-improvement review now.

- `/status`, `/context`, `/agents`: session info, a context-window breakdown, and running tasks.

## Configuration commands

- `/config`: show your current configuration.

- `/reasoning [level]`: set reasoning effort, from none up to max or ultra.

- `/fast`: fast mode (OpenAI Priority Processing / Anthropic Fast Mode).

- `/personality` and `/skin`: change the agent’s personality or the display theme.

- `/verbose` and `/focus`: show more or less tool output.

- `/busy`: decide what happens when you message while Hermes is working: queue, steer or interrupt.

- `/approvals [manual|smart|off]` and `/yolo`: control approval prompts for risky commands. Be careful with /yolo, which skips them all.

- `/voice` and `/wake`: voice mode and the “Hey Hermes” wake word.

- `/export` and `/import`: pack a profile into a shareable archive, or install one (CLI only).

## Tools and skills commands

- `/tools` and `/toolsets`: list, enable or disable tools for this session.

- `/skills`: search, install and manage skills, and approve skill changes.

- `/learn <source>`: turn a folder, a link or a workflow you just did into a reusable skill.

- `/plan [task]`: write a plan to `.hermes/plans/` without doing anything.

- `/init`: generate an AGENTS.md from a repo scan.

- `/cron`, `/blueprint`, `/suggestions`: scheduled tasks, automation templates and suggested automations.

- `/memory`: review memory writes waiting for approval.

- `/kanban`: drive the multi-profile project board from chat.

- `/browser connect`: attach browser tools to your running Chrome, Brave, Chromium or Edge.

- `/plugins`, `/reload-mcp`, `/reload-skills`, `/reload`: check plugins and reload MCP servers, skills or.env keys.

Want this set up for you instead of doing it yourself? Claim your free strategy session →

Claim Your Free SEO Strategy Session →

## Info and account commands

- `/help` and `/palette`: find any command.

- `/usage`, `/insights`: usage now and over the last 30 days.

- `/subscription` and `/topup`: your Nous plan and balance.

- `/login`: sign in with a Nous account.

- `/version`, `/profile`, `/whoami`: version, active profile and your command access level.

- `/paste`, `/image <path>`, `/copy`: attach images or copy the last answer.

- `/update` and `/debug`: update Hermes or upload a debug report.

- `/quit` (or `/exit`): leave the CLI.

## Slash commands in Telegram, Discord and Slack

Most commands work the same in messaging apps. A few only exist there, according to the reference:

- `/approve` and `/deny`: approve or reject a risky command waiting for you.

items.content:
To migrate OpenClaw to Hermes, you install one official plugin and run one command: `hermes import-agent openclaw`. It copies your persona, memory, skills, model settings, MCP servers and messaging bots from `~/.openclaw` into Hermes, and it always shows you a preview before it changes anything. Since Hermes Agent v0.22.5 (22 October 2026), this lives in the official `agent-importers` plugin instead of the core app. The older command, `hermes claw migrate`, still works and does exactly the same thing. Below is the full process from the official migration guide, in plain English: the safe test run, what moves over and what doesn’t, how API keys work, and the checklist to run afterwards. I’ve also put my Hermes vs OpenClaw test video below.

Key takeaways

- Install once: `hermes plugins install agent-importers`.

- Test first: `hermes import-agent openclaw --dry-run` changes nothing.

- API keys only come over if you add –migrate-secrets.

- A backup of `~/.hermes` is saved before anything is written.

- Want your agents moved and set up for you? Claim a free strategy session.

## What “migrate OpenClaw to Hermes” actually means

OpenClaw and Hermes Agent are both personal AI agents that run on your own machine or server, keep memory, use skills and talk to you on apps like Telegram and Discord. If you’ve built up an OpenClaw setup over months, the hard part of switching isn’t installing Hermes. It’s rebuilding everything your agent already knows.

The migration tool does that rebuild for you. According to the Hermes CLI reference, it covers more than 30 categories across persona, memory, skills, model providers, messaging platforms, agent behaviour, session policies, MCP servers and text-to-speech. Each item is either imported directly into its Hermes equivalent or archived so you can review it by hand.

It also finds older installs. If you started on Clawdbot or Moltbot, the tool checks `~/.clawdbot` and `~/.moltbot` automatically, plus the old config names `clawdbot.json` and `moltbot.json`.

## The easy way: let Hermes setup do it

If you’re installing Hermes fresh on a machine that already has OpenClaw, you may not need any commands at all. The guide says that when you run `hermes setup` and it finds `~/.openclaw`, it asks “Import your setup from OpenClaw?”

Say yes and setup installs the plugin, runs the import with your API keys included, shows you the preview, asks you to confirm, and then carries on with the parts of setup the import didn’t cover. If the import brought over a model and its key, Quick Setup then asks whether you want to keep that model or switch to Nous Portal.

Already have Hermes configured? Use the manual steps below instead.

## How to migrate OpenClaw to Hermes step by step

These are the commands from the Quick start, in the order I’d run them:

- 1. Install the plugin (once per profile): `hermes plugins install agent-importers`

- 2. Do a test run: `hermes import-agent openclaw --dry-run`. This shows what would move over and stops. Nothing is written.

- 3. Run the real migration: `hermes import-agent openclaw`. It shows the full preview again, then asks you to confirm.

- 4. Bring your API keys too (optional): `hermes import-agent openclaw --preset full --migrate-secrets`

- 5. Start a new session so the imported skills and memory load.

Before it writes anything, Hermes saves one restore-point zip of `~/.hermes` to `~/.hermes/backups/pre-migration-*.zip`. If something goes wrong you can restore it with `hermes import`. You can skip that backup with `--no-backup`, but I wouldn’t.

Not comfortable in the terminal? Ask your agent: “Install the agent-importers plugin, do a dry run of the OpenClaw import, and show me what would move over before you change anything.”

## Every migration option explained

Option
What it does

–dry-run
Preview only. Nothing is written.

–preset full
All compatible settings (still no API keys).

–preset user-data
Your data without infrastructure config (still no API keys).

–migrate-secrets
Include API keys. Needed even with –preset full.

–overwrite
Replace existing Hermes files on conflicts. By default the import refuses to apply when there are conflicts.

–no-backup
Skip the pre-migration zip of ~/.hermes.

–source <path>
Use an OpenClaw folder somewhere other than ~/.openclaw.

–workspace-target <path>
Where to put your AGENTS.md workspace instructions.

–skill-conflict
skip (default), overwrite, or rename when a skill name already exists.

–yes
Skip the confirmation prompt after the preview.

The safety rule worth remembering: no preset ever imports your API keys silently. You have to type `--migrate-secrets` on purpose.

## What moves over from OpenClaw (and where it lands)

The migration guide lists exactly where each piece ends up. The main ones:

From OpenClaw
To Hermes

workspace/SOUL.md (persona)
~/.hermes/SOUL.md

workspace/MEMORY.md and daily memory files
~/.hermes/memories/MEMORY.md (merged, duplicates removed)

workspace/USER.md
~/.hermes/memories/USER.md

workspace/AGENTS.md
AGENTS.md in your –workspace-target folder

Skills from 4 places
~/.hermes/skills/openclaw-imports/

Default model and custom providers
config.yaml

MCP servers
mcp_servers in config.yaml

Telegram, Discord, Slack, WhatsApp, Signal, Matrix and Mattermost tokens and allowlists
~/.hermes/.env

TTS voice settings (ElevenLabs, OpenAI, Edge)
tts in config.yaml

Agent behaviour is translated too. For example, OpenClaw’s thinking level becomes Hermes’ reasoning effort (“high”, “medium” or “low”), your timezone and Docker sandbox settings carry over, and compression settings map across.

## What doesn’t move over automatically

Some things are archived for manual review rather than imported. The guide lists cron jobs, plugins, hooks and webhooks, the QMD memory backend, the skills registry config, UI and identity settings, logging, multi-agent setups, channel bindings, and the files IDENTITY.md, TOOLS.md, HEARTBEAT.md and BOOTSTRAP.md.

You’ll find them in `~/.hermes/migration/openclaw/<timestamp>/archive/`. The ones most people will want to redo by hand are cron jobs, since scheduled tasks are usually where an agent earns its keep.

Two more things to know:

- Idle and daily reset timers are not imported. In Hermes a conversation carries on until you type `/new` or `/reset`.

- WhatsApp needs re-pairing. It uses QR-code pairing, not a token, so run `hermes whatsapp` after the migration.

## How API keys are found and moved

When you pass `--migrate-secrets`, Hermes looks for keys in three places, in this order: your OpenClaw config values, then `~/.openclaw/.env`, then `auth-profiles.json`. Token fields can be plain text, environment templates like `${VAR}`, or OpenClaw SecretRef objects, and the tool handles all three.

Keys go into `~/.hermes/.env`. Afterwards, run `hermes status` to check each provider signs in properly.

## After you migrate: the checklist

The guide gives an 8-step check. In short:

- Read the migration report: it counts what was migrated, skipped and in conflict.

- Review the archived files in the migration folder.

- Start a new session. Imported skills and memory only load in new sessions.

- Run `hermes status` to verify API keys.

- Restart the gateway if you moved bot tokens: `systemctl --user restart hermes-gateway`

- Check the archived session settings.

- Re-pair WhatsApp with `hermes whatsapp`.

- When everything works, run `hermes claw cleanup`. It renames the old OpenClaw folders to `.pre-migration`.

Careful: after `hermes claw cleanup`, OpenClaw itself stops working because its folders have been renamed. Rename them back if you need to undo it.

## Fixing common migration problems

- “OpenClaw directory not found”: your install is somewhere unusual. Add `--source /path/to/your/openclaw`.

- “No provider API keys found”: keys can live in several places depending on your OpenClaw version. Make sure you passed `--migrate-secrets`.

- Skills not showing up: they’re in `~/.hermes/skills/openclaw-imports/`. Start a new session, or type `/skills` to check they loaded.

- TTS voice missing: if you set the voice in OpenClaw’s UI it may be stored somewhere the tool doesn’t read. Set it again with `hermes config set`.

## Moving from Claude Code, Codex or Cursor too

The same plugin imports more than OpenClaw. `hermes import-agent claude-code`, `codex` or `cursor` bring over instructions and rules as memory entries, permission rules as allowlists, MCP servers and skills, as the import guide explains. For those three agents, credentials are never imported, and `--sync` re-imports a source later if it changed.

So if you’ve been running OpenClaw for your messaging bots and Claude Code for coding, Hermes can pull in both.

## My verdict

This is the cleanest way to switch I’ve seen from any agent: a test run that changes nothing, a backup before every write, API keys only when you ask, and a clear list of what you’ll need to redo by hand. Do the dry run, read the report, rebuild your cron jobs, and you’re done. If you’ve been waiting to migrate OpenClaw to Hermes, you can now do it in one sitting.

## About Julian Goldie

I’m Julian Goldie — founder of Goldie Agency and the AI Profit Boardroom. I test new AI agents almost every day for 432K+ YouTube subscribers and run Hermes, OpenClaw, OpenCode, Claude and Codex side by side in my own Agent OS. Claim your free strategy session or join the AI Profit Boardroom.

Want another angle? Read the AI Profit Boardroom guide to Migrating OpenClaw to Hermes.

## FAQ: migrate openclaw to hermes

### How do I migrate OpenClaw to Hermes?

Install the agent-importers plugin with hermes plugins install agent-importers, preview with hermes import-agent openclaw –dry-run, then run hermes import-agent openclaw. Add –migrate-secrets if you want your API keys moved too.

### Is hermes claw migrate still available?

Yes. hermes claw migrate is the older spelling of hermes import-agent openclaw and does exactly the same thing. Both now come from the official agent-importers plugin.

### Does the migration copy my API keys?

Only if you pass –migrate-secrets. No preset imports secrets on its own, not even –preset full.

### Will migrating break my OpenClaw install?

No. The import only reads from OpenClaw. OpenClaw stops working only if you later run hermes claw cleanup, which renames its folders; you can rename them back to undo it.

### Are my OpenClaw cron jobs migrated?

No. Cron jobs, plugins, hooks and a few other items are archived for manual review in ~/.hermes/migration/openclaw//archive/, so you set them up again in Hermes.

### Can I undo a migration?

Yes. Before applying, Hermes saves a zip of ~/.hermes to ~/.hermes/backups/pre-migration-*.zip, which you can restore with hermes import.

Below is the full process from the official migration guide, in plain English: the safe test run, what moves over and what doesn’t, how API keys work, and the checklist to run afterwards. I’ve also put my Hermes vs OpenClaw test video below.

Key takeaways

  • Install once: hermes plugins install agent-importers.
  • Test first: hermes import-agent openclaw --dry-run changes nothing.
  • API keys only come over if you add –migrate-secrets.
  • A backup of ~/.hermes is saved before anything is written.

What “migrate OpenClaw to Hermes” actually means

OpenClaw and Hermes Agent are both personal AI agents that run on your own machine or server, keep memory, use skills and talk to you on apps like Telegram and Discord. If you’ve built up an OpenClaw setup over months, the hard part of switching isn’t installing Hermes. It’s rebuilding everything your agent already knows.

The migration tool does that rebuild for you. According to the Hermes CLI reference, it covers more than 30 categories across persona, memory, skills, model providers, messaging platforms, agent behaviour, session policies, MCP servers and text-to-speech. Each item is either imported directly into its Hermes equivalent or archived so you can review it by hand.

It also finds older installs. If you started on Clawdbot or Moltbot, the tool checks ~/.clawdbot and ~/.moltbot automatically, plus the old config names clawdbot.json and moltbot.json.

The easy way: let Hermes setup do it

If you’re installing Hermes fresh on a machine that already has OpenClaw, you may not need any commands at all. The guide says that when you run hermes setup and it finds ~/.openclaw, it asks “Import your setup from OpenClaw?”

Say yes and setup installs the plugin, runs the import with your API keys included, shows you the preview, asks you to confirm, and then carries on with the parts of setup the import didn’t cover. If the import brought over a model and its key, Quick Setup then asks whether you want to keep that model or switch to Nous Portal.

How to migrate OpenClaw to Hermes step by step

These are the commands from the Quick start, in the order I’d run them:

  • 1. Install the plugin (once per profile): hermes plugins install agent-importers
  • 2. Do a test run: hermes import-agent openclaw --dry-run. This shows what would move over and stops. Nothing is written.
  • 3. Run the real migration: hermes import-agent openclaw. It shows the full preview again, then asks you to confirm.
  • 4. Bring your API keys too (optional): hermes import-agent openclaw --preset full --migrate-secrets
  • 5. Start a new session so the imported skills and memory load.

Before it writes anything, Hermes saves one restore-point zip of ~/.hermes to ~/.hermes/backups/pre-migration-*.zip. If something goes wrong you can restore it with hermes import. You can skip that backup with --no-backup, but I wouldn’t.

Not comfortable in the terminal? Ask your agent: “Install the agent-importers plugin, do a dry run of the OpenClaw import, and show me what would move over before you change anything.”

Every migration option explained

Option

What it does

–dry-run

Preview only. Nothing is written.

–preset full

All compatible settings (still no API keys).

–preset user-data

Your data without infrastructure config (still no API keys).

–migrate-secrets

Include API keys. Needed even with –preset full.

–overwrite

Replace existing Hermes files on conflicts. By default the import refuses to apply when there are conflicts.

–no-backup

Skip the pre-migration zip of ~/.hermes.

–source

Use an OpenClaw folder somewhere other than ~/.openclaw.

–workspace-target

Where to put your AGENTS.md workspace instructions.

–skill-conflict

skip (default), overwrite, or rename when a skill name already exists.

–yes

Skip the confirmation prompt after the preview.

The safety rule worth remembering: no preset ever imports your API keys silently. You have to type --migrate-secrets on purpose.

What doesn’t move over automatically

Some things are archived for manual review rather than imported. The guide lists cron jobs, plugins, hooks and webhooks, the QMD memory backend, the skills registry config, UI and identity settings, logging, multi-agent setups, channel bindings, and the files IDENTITY.md, TOOLS.md, HEARTBEAT.md and BOOTSTRAP.md.

You’ll find them in ~/.hermes/migration/openclaw//archive/. The ones most people will want to redo by hand are cron jobs, since scheduled tasks are usually where an agent earns its keep.

Two more things to know:

  • Idle and daily reset timers are not imported. In Hermes a conversation carries on until you type /new or /reset.
  • WhatsApp needs re-pairing. It uses QR-code pairing, not a token, so run hermes whatsapp after the migration.

How API keys are found and moved

When you pass --migrate-secrets, Hermes looks for keys in three places, in this order: your OpenClaw config values, then ~/.openclaw/.env, then auth-profiles.json. Token fields can be plain text, environment templates like ${VAR}, or OpenClaw SecretRef objects, and the tool handles all three.

Keys go into ~/.hermes/.env. Afterwards, run hermes status to check each provider signs in properly.

After you migrate: the checklist

The guide gives an 8-step check. In short:

  • Read the migration report: it counts what was migrated, skipped and in conflict.
  • Review the archived files in the migration folder.
  • Start a new session. Imported skills and memory only load in new sessions.
  • Run hermes status to verify API keys.
  • Restart the gateway if you moved bot tokens: systemctl --user restart hermes-gateway
  • Check the archived session settings.
  • Re-pair WhatsApp with hermes whatsapp.
  • When everything works, run hermes claw cleanup. It renames the old OpenClaw folders to .pre-migration.

Careful: after hermes claw cleanup, OpenClaw itself stops working because its folders have been renamed. Rename them back if you need to undo it.

Fixing common migration problems

  • “OpenClaw directory not found”: your install is somewhere unusual. Add --source /path/to/your/openclaw.
  • “No provider API keys found”: keys can live in several places depending on your OpenClaw version. Make sure you passed --migrate-secrets.
  • Skills not showing up: they’re in ~/.hermes/skills/openclaw-imports/. Start a new session, or type /skills to check they loaded.
  • TTS voice missing: if you set the voice in OpenClaw’s UI it may be stored somewhere the tool doesn’t read. Set it again with hermes config set.

Moving from Claude Code, Codex or Cursor too

The same plugin imports more than OpenClaw. hermes import-agent claude-code, codex or cursor bring over instructions and rules as memory entries, permission rules as allowlists, MCP servers and skills, as the import guide explains. For those three agents, credentials are never imported, and --sync re-imports a source later if it changed.

So if you’ve been running OpenClaw for your messaging bots and Claude Code for coding, Hermes can pull in both.

My verdict

This is the cleanest way to switch I’ve seen from any agent: a test run that changes nothing, a backup before every write, API keys only when you ask, and a clear list of what you’ll need to redo by hand. Do the dry run, read the report, rebuild your cron jobs, and you’re done. If you’ve been waiting to migrate OpenClaw to Hermes, you can now do it in one sitting.

FAQ: migrate openclaw to hermes

How do I migrate OpenClaw to Hermes?

Install the agent-importers plugin with hermes plugins install agent-importers, preview with hermes import-agent openclaw –dry-run, then run hermes import-agent openclaw. Add –migrate-secrets if you want your API keys moved too.

Is hermes claw migrate still available?

Yes. hermes claw migrate is the older spelling of hermes import-agent openclaw and does exactly the same thing. Both now come from the official agent-importers plugin.

Does the migration copy my API keys?

Only if you pass –migrate-secrets. No preset imports secrets on its own, not even –preset full.

Will migrating break my OpenClaw install?

No. The import only reads from OpenClaw. OpenClaw stops working only if you later run hermes claw cleanup, which renames its folders; you can rename them back to undo it.

Are my OpenClaw cron jobs migrated?

No. Cron jobs, plugins, hooks and a few other items are archived for manual review in ~/.hermes/migration/openclaw//archive/, so you set them up again in Hermes.

Can I undo a migration?

Yes. Before applying, Hermes saves a zip of ~/.hermes to ~/.hermes/backups/pre-migration-*.zip, which you can restore with hermes import.

items.title: Show HN: I built a Claude Code plugin to query 10.6M earnings-call embeddings
items.content:
Hi HN,

I've been using LLMs for one-off market questions against a database of earnings transcripts since ~2025. In tech years that's a long time so as a Solo dev I built a platform around it and have been adding miscellaneous other financial tools and integrations. Backend infrastructure is super boring! PostgreSQL & ElasticSearch, with the data appropriately sharded and replicated across two regions.

Some example requests:

"What did NVIDIA say about data-center demand
